planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; gold speckling is densest and brightest with little or no direct sun.

directions: Golden Spangles bears glossy, leathery dark green leaves finely speckled all over with small flecks of gold, giving a lighter, more evenly dappled effect than the bolder blotching of Crotonifolia. It forms a dense, rounded, slower-growing bush that holds its compact habit with little pruning, making it useful where a tidy evergreen is needed under trees or along shaded foundations. Female plants set small red berries in winter when a male aucuba grows nearby, and like other aucubas it tolerates deep, dry shade and poor soil that would stress most broadleaf evergreens.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, away from direct midday sun.

directions: February Star carries narrower, more finely toothed leaves than typical aucuba cultivars, marked with only a light scatter of pale yellow dots rather than the heavy gold blotching of more common selections, giving it a more refined, lower-key look in shaded plantings. It is a female clone and produces small red winter berries when a male aucuba grows within pollination range. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, where it tolerates the dry shade under mature trees better than most broadleaf evergreens.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun; the purple coloring on stems and leaf stalks holds up well even in fairly shaded sites.

directions: Purple Shaft holds an Award of Garden Merit for its persistently dark purple-black young stems and leaf stalks, a trait that lingers through the season rather than fading to green the way the transient purple spring flush on other false holly cultivars does. Its spiny, holly-like leaves are glossy dark green, and in fall it produces the tiny, intensely sweet-scented white flowers typical of the species, easy to smell from several feet away even though the blooms themselves are inconspicuous. It forms a dense, slow-growing, deer-resistant screen or informal hedge and asks for little beyond well-drained, humus-rich soil and an occasional light shaping after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic soil sheltered from drying winter wind.

directions: Madame Briot is a female English holly with spiny, glossy dark green leaves broadly margined in rich gold, a classic variegated selection that has been grown in European estate gardens since the Victorian era and holds an Award of Garden Merit. It sets a heavy crop of bright red berries in fall and winter when a male holly grows within pollinator range, and its dense, pyramidal habit needs little shaping to stay tidy. Site it in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with some shelter from harsh winter sun and wind, which can scorch variegated foliage, and prune lightly in late winter if a more formal outline is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic soil; as a male clone it sets no berries but is useful as a pollinator and specimen.

directions: Despite its name, Golden Queen is a male English holly, one of the long-grown Award of Garden Merit cultivars with broad, spiny leaves edged in creamy gold and new growth often tinged pink-bronze before settling to green and gold. Because it carries no berries, it earns its place as a reliable pollinator for nearby female gold-variegated hollies as well as a dense, year-round accent plant in its own right. Grow in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil with some protection from scorching winter sun and wind, and shape with light pruning after the new growth hardens off.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic soil; this slow-growing novelty holly is usually sited as a specimen rather than massed.

directions: The Silver Hedgehog Holly is a centuries-old novelty cultivar whose small leaves curl sharply upward and carry extra spines scattered across the leaf surface itself in addition to the usual marginal spines, giving each leaf a bristling, hedgehog-like texture, further set off by a narrow silvery-white leaf margin. It is a male clone and produces no berries, grown instead for its distinctive, slow-growing, densely twiggy form as a conversation-piece specimen in shaded or partially shaded borders. Plant in well-drained, acidic soil sheltered from harsh winter wind and prune only to remove the occasional reverted plain-green shoot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic soil; a male holly nearby is needed for berry set.

directions: Amber is a female English holly, an Award of Garden Merit selection grown for berries that ripen to a warm amber-orange rather than the typical glossy red of most hollies, giving a softer, less common color note in winter plantings. Its glossy, spiny dark green leaves and dense, upright habit are otherwise typical of the species, making it easy to work into mixed shrub borders or hedgerows. Grow in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil with a male holly within pollinating range, and shelter from harsh winter sun and wind to avoid leaf scorch.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile soil; tolerates shade, salt spray, and urban pollution better than most variegated hollies.

directions: Golden King is, despite the name, a female clone of the Highclere holly group, a hybrid between English and Madeiran hollies bred for large, nearly spineless leaves broadly margined in gold around a gray-green center. It sets a heavy crop of red berries each fall without needing a particularly fussy pollination partner, and it grows into one of the most widely planted large-leaved variegated hollies in gardens and churchyard plantings. It tolerates shade, coastal exposure, and urban pollution better than most hollies, asking only for reasonably well-drained soil and an occasional trim to keep a dense screen or specimen shape.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile soil; a long-grown large-leaved holly suited to screening in partial shade.

directions: Lawsoniana arose as a sport of the Highclere holly group and is distinguished from relatives like Golden King by its gold-yellow variegation sitting as an irregular central blotch on each leaf rather than running along the margin, so the leaf edge stays plain dark green. It is a female clone that produces red berries in fall, carried on large, mostly spineless leaves typical of the altaclerensis hybrids. This vigorous, long-cultivated holly tolerates partial shade, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it a dependable choice for dense screening or as a lawn specimen.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile soil; vigorous and shade-tolerant, well suited to tall hedging or screening.

directions: Camelliifolia is named for its very large, glossy, nearly spineless dark green leaves, which resemble camellia foliage more than typical spiny holly leaves, carried on young stems and petioles flushed deep purple. It is a vigorous, female Highclere holly that sets a heavy crop of red berries each fall and grows quickly into a dense, substantial shrub or small tree useful for tall screening and windbreaks. It tolerates partial shade, wind, and urban pollution well, and like other altaclerensis hollies needs only well-drained, reasonably fertile soil and occasional shaping to keep its size in check.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile soil; tolerates coastal exposure and shade better than most variegated hollies.

directions: Belgica Aurea is a female Highclere holly with softer gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy yellow-gold, less heavily spined than typical English holly, giving a gentler-textured variegated accent in the landscape. It sets red berries in fall when pollinated and grows into a dense, upright, vigorous shrub well suited to large hedges, screens, or specimen planting. It is notably tolerant of partial shade, coastal wind, and salt spray, needing only well-drained soil and occasional pruning to control its eventual size.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; a low, spreading groundcover-style holly useful as a boxwood substitute.

directions: Green Lustre is a low, dense, wide-spreading Japanese holly with small, glossy, spineless dark green leaves that hold their color through winter without the bronzing some other crenata cultivars show. Its mounded, horizontally branching habit makes it useful as a low hedge, foundation planting, or large-scale groundcover where a fine-textured, boxwood-like evergreen is wanted. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly after flush growth hardens if a tighter form is preferred.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; a long-popular, larger-growing boxwood-substitute selection.

directions: Hetzii is a long-grown Japanese holly cultivar with dense, compact, rounded growth and small, glossy dark green leaves lacking visible spines, forming a sturdy evergreen mound larger and somewhat looser than dwarf selections like Helleri or Compacta. It has been a mainstay foundation and hedging shrub in American landscapes for decades, prized as a dependable boxwood substitute where boxwood blight or leafminer are concerns. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun and shear or hand-prune as needed to maintain a formal or informal shape.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; a dense semi-dwarf selection popular for low foundation hedges.

directions: Chesapeake is a semi-dwarf Japanese holly with a dense, rounded, slow-spreading habit and small, glossy, spineless dark green leaves that keep the look of clipped boxwood with far less maintenance. It stays notably compact and uniform without heavy shearing, which has made it a popular low hedge and foundation shrub in mid-Atlantic and southern landscapes. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first year or two while roots establish.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Stallion is a vigorous male pollinator and produces no berries itself.

directions: Blue Stallion is a vigorous male selection in the blue holly group, bred as a more upright, faster-growing pollinator counterpart to Blue Prince for the popular female Blue Princess and Blue Girl hollies. Its small, spiny, glossy blue-green leaves emerge on blue-purple young stems and hold their color well through cold winters that can bronze other broadleaf evergreens. Because it is a male clone it never fruits, but planting one within range of several female Blue-series hollies ensures reliable berry set on the females. Grow in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, with minimal pruning needed beyond shaping.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered spot in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Gurkha is a notably cold-hardy, high-elevation clone that tends to lose more of its leaves in hard winters than Jacqueline Postill.

directions: Gurkha was selected from high-elevation Himalayan daphne collected in cold, exposed terrain, and it carries an Award of Garden Merit for being noticeably more cold-hardy than most Daphne bholua forms sold in the trade. In late winter it opens clusters of intensely fragrant, pale pink-flushed white flowers on upright bare or sparsely leaved stems, scenting the garden well before most other shrubs stir. It is more deciduous in hard winters than evergreen selections like Jacqueline Postill, dropping leaves under cold stress but flowering reliably regardless. Site it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, partially shaded spot, and avoid disturbing its roots once established; all parts are toxic if ingested.
